activity.title: Semester recap and offer post? 💙💛💙 Around 60% of this semester I spent studying quantum mechanics (and about 20% more on two other math courses + TA-ing linear algebra). Fall is also application season, and balancing interviews with solving QM problems felt like trying to measure two incompatible observables. But God had the best plan for me. It all started when I freaked out because I realized CodeSignal attempts are not infinite, and I had used my last one late at night, solving problems “for fun” with no prep. The score wasn’t my highest, and I was so discouraged I almost stopped applying altogether. I submitted it anyway. Somewhat unexpectedly, that still led to four interviews with Gusto . I wore my Boca Juniors jersey with Ander Herrera #21 on the back to every single one because it helped me calm down. Not the most traditional interview strategy, but it became my little ritual. By the time interviews came around, I hadn’t touched LeetCode in months because of my course load, so I only prepped for two days. But everything I’d built over the last two years, including staying up until 4am for CodePath sessions, paid off :) That’s it, sometimes one chance is enough when it’s the right one. I’m very grateful for God’s support throughout this process. Sooo, happy to share that I’ll be joining Gusto in SF this summer as a SWE intern. Thank you to Janielle Rodriguez for guiding me through the recruiting process with so much clarity and kindness. Thank you to Mohanad and Temilola for their support, to Islam for having had a big influence on my coding journey since freshman year, and to everyone who did mock interviews with me at some point in my life. And of course, thank you, Manchester United , for a 5-game unbeaten streak that somehow aligned perfectly with my whole Gusto interview process. Elite timing, because we’ve gone downhill again now. I really hope everyone gets what they truly deserve, good luck everyone!!🫶🫶 P.S. Drew this illustration, procrastinating on my assignments. ...more

This semester, I was involved in a project developing the n-Copilot (copilot for nurses) at Jubo Health Technologies in Taipei, Taiwan. This journey was full of ups and downs for me, but it was a unique experience that improved my technical skills and stress-resilience, and introduced me to the world of healthcare technology — a field I never imagined I'd work in. Over these 3 months, I deepened my technical knowledge by developing a new module and functions for the copilot to efficiently manage HR-related queries. Along the way, we presented our work at a seminar at National Taiwan University and at Minerva University Symposium. The highlight of the progress was showcasing our project at Healthcare+ Expo Taiwan (Dec 5-6) that attracted over 70,000 visitors from around the world. Looking back, those weekly demos and biweekly presentations to the team were intense, but it was an interesting experience. From debugging late at night to celebrating small wins — every moment contributed to my growth and learning. Thank you, my teammates — Islam Assanov , Amina Rakhimbergenova , and Youran Zhao — for making this journey unforgettable. Special gratitude to Prof. Tsai, Yun-Huei Pan , Will, and Dr. Jessy Kang for providing this opportunity! ...more

This summer, I was accepted to Mastercard 's summer internship program in Kazakhstan. Over two intense months, I immersed myself in a project focusing on AI adoption in banking – a field entirely new to me. Despite my non-banking background, I used my technical skills to develop a comprehensive solution: a website presenting my research findings, an in-depth report, and an AI adoption assessment tool for banks. This tool evaluates a bank's current AI implementation level, provides tailored feedback, and offers specific recommendations for improvement of AI adoption within different departments in banks. As a result, I finished among the top 3 interns in the program. This journey wouldn't have been possible without the guidance of my mentor, Aigerim Garifullina . Her support was very important in helping me navigate this new field and excel in my project. I'm also incredibly grateful to AIESEC in Kazakhstan , the Mastercard team, and my fellow interns for creating such a rich and collaborative learning environment. Reflecting on this experience, I'm grateful for how much I've grown both professionally and personally. As I move forward in my career, I'm eager to build on this foundation, take on new challenges, and continue exploring new opportunities for growth. ...more

AI coding agents are getting powerful fast - but do you actually understand end to end what they did? I noticed I was mostly just trusting the Claude Code's output. There's no real visibility into what changed, why, or whether any of it was actually verified. I built TraceBack -> a VS Code extension that gives you observability and control over Claude Code sessions, without leaving your editor. — Each prompt becomes a chapter, so your session is organized and reviewable without scrolling through a wall of terminal output. All past sessions in one place. — File diffs per file, same as GitHub's, but with the agent's reasoning and a badge showing whether it actually tested its own edits — A tab that surfaces the decisions and assumptions the agent made mid-session, before they break — Guards that block dangerous operations like rm -rf or git push main before they run — Pause a live agent at its next action and redirect it mid-session — Export the full session in beautifully formatted JSON, Markdown, or HTML when you're done Runs entirely local, no API keys and no SDKs. 🏘️ Let me live in your village for days! I’m making an intentional village where villagers know neighbors well, share things together, kids get to experience and learn from experience, and the whole village raises children together with love and warmth. Building many villages like this is the biggest dream of my life. And I am about to take my first journey to make it happen. Hi, I’m Youngeun – I introduce myself as Young n old “young” & “en”, a rising senior at Minerva University . I am obsessed with parenting and believe if the world is happy, everyone would like to become a parent. I believe true happiness comes from healthy love and community. Why am I so curious about parenting in my 20s? I view the world from the perspective of love and attachment. Babies need full attention and sensitive and immediate response from their parents. It is important to realize that family is a comfort zone and they will love you unconditionally. To do this, parents need to have a huge emotional capacity. Even if you know that you should not neglect the baby or respond discontinuously depending on your mood, if you don’t have that emotional bandwidth to digest your immediate emotion, you may react without thinking. When parenting is done in a close community, the burden of one parent can be lower. When you are busy, other neighbors could take care of the baby or play in a safe place with friends. Parents feel safe that there is someone looking after my child. However, nowadays, villages with a close community like this are few and far between . We’ve become accustomed to an apartment where we don’t know who is living next door. Friends and family live far away. This is why I want to bring back that humane, warm, close community through making villages so that stable love can flourish across the generations. 🌷To begin my journey of making villages, I plan to visit villages all around the world that have a close community and/or an alternative education curriculum. This trip is going to happen in September! If you know any of the villages that has their own culture to hold their community close and connected and/or has an alternative education system attached to it, please let me know. I would love to visit! If you know/visited/lived in/live in an intentional village, please let me know, I will truly appreciate it! If you found yourself interested in my point of view and want to talk more about it, please feel free to dm me. I’m more than happy to connect with you:D Feel free to share this post or tag someone who might be interested in this below!

LinkedIn scares me. Partly because every time I open it, a deprecating feeling of being behind washes over me. And partly because I've never written much on my own on here. But now's as good a time as any. So, some things from my 20ish-year journey on this 4.5 billion-year-old planet. I'm currently in SF interning at AdaL , wearing many hats: growth, design, video, and talking too much about AI harnesses. I make story-driven content on Instagram about travel, culture, and being an international student, but I hate it when people call me an influencer. I'm also a student at Minerva University , and within 3 years I've lived in 5 countries. From bustling techy San Francisco, to the boba motherland and geopolitically peculiar island of Taiwan, to media-homogenized Seoul, to the ice-cream heaven and shaken economy of Buenos Aires, to the biriyani capital Hyderabad, and soon the beer-and-pretzel land of Berlin. I can't fit three years of observations/learnings from my nomadic college experience into one post, but here's a start: → Everything is figure-out-able. If you’re stuck in a random Taiwanese city with no connection in the dark or don’t have a place to sleep while on a solo trip in the Southwest of India, the instinct is to quickly strategize and treat these mishaps as fun stories to tell. This mindset extends to work: if I don’t know how to do something, well, I thank the internet and my flow state and try to master Adobe Illustrator in one evening. → People are more open than I expected. On a solo trip in Vietnam , I talked to 15+ strangers, each time after a 10-second internal debate over whether to approach that fellow solo-traveler or cool-dressed uncle. 0/10 times was I greeted poorly, and 10/10 times I had a heartwarming conversation with people I’d met 6 minutes ago. This ability to connect with even a brick wall has led to conversations on topics far more riveting than AI B2B SaaS at networking events. → Nuance is critical. To understand a place, you have to understand its context and where it comes from (same principle goes for people): from its colonial history and religious divide to its industrial systems. This approach to travel made me notice the hidden beauty of a quaint alleyway, or, conversely, the grandiose ambition behind a 140-meter avenue. → Ambiguity is exploration. I’ve gotten used to not speaking the local language and instead relying on a month's worth of Duolingo to help me maneuver a city. It’s no longer uncomfortable to be linguistically clueless but a fun challenge of “how can I communicate through Google Translate, emoting, and heavy gesticulation?” Part 2 coming (I hit the word limit here). But for now, cheers to the beauty of the human experience: how much we can pull from random moments, and how differently the world looks depending on where you point your attention (though mine is currently on my 560-day Duolingo streak). Keep being human and seeing the world through your unique lens :)

As I wrap up my sophomore year, I’m excited to share that I joined Cloudflare as a Strategy Operations Intern in San Francisco this summer, serving the Procurement team. Joining right after a major ERP migration meant an incredible learning curve. I was always encouraged to own end-to-end initiatives, and was also empowered to work on 3 different projects, including: translating legal intakes into PRDs for an internal AI Redline tool; leveraging MCP to help sync enterprise data across platforms; and collaborating with the engineering team to build an automated anomaly-flagging feature for a dashboard. Words cannot describe how grateful I am for the mentorship and empowerment I received from the leadership team: Darrell R. Deams, CIA, CFE, Rudy Saenz , and Jacob Paradeis , for always giving me structured guidance and the autonomy to build. So many people to honor, and you're definitely a part of the support network I am deeply grateful for: my friends, my mentors, and faculty. Thank you for making my 2nd year truly unforgettable. Proud to have contributed to Cloudflare’s mission: Building a Better Internet! 🚀

: what did you do during this july 4th shutdown? : emmmm i went to the office and studied… not necessarily because im asian, but because… I find work so unfamiliar yet strangely and genuinely interesting. there is still so much i don’t know and this break is the time for me to fill that knowledge gap - unbothered by new tasks, meetings, and commute, but simply sit, with my brain, my computer, a whiteboard, and bunch of question marks in my head, ready to get answered. this summer, I joined LinkedIn as a SWE intern working in the GPU and ML Training Team under the AI Infra Org, where I work with three other interns on kernel optimizations for NVIDIA ’s Blackwell GPU architecture. as best friends with Python, and without any computer architecture prerequisite (and none are offered at Minerva either way), I found myself ascending on an extremely steep learning curve: hearing about kernel programming languages and distributed training terms and frameworks for the first time, constantly messing up the CuDA thread hierarchy, and semi-embarrassingly admitting 𝗔 𝗟𝗢𝗧 of things that I don’t know. but then I find comfort. comfort in saying that I didn’t know, of being honest to myself and to the people who have entrusted me with responsibilities. i realized that saying no is saying yes. saying yes to myself that i have such a knowledge gap to fill, that im capable of filling it as long as i take actions. and this week was the testament. a testament where I finally (somewhat) untangled some knots on what prefill/decode are in RL, how tiling and layouts work in CuTe, and how pipelining / warp specialization can help solve a lot RL throughout and GPU utilization bottlenecks. at this halfway point of summer, while people are sharing their takeaways from their internships thus far, I find myself, quite the opposite - i still struggled to extrapolate these lessons. i still feel the burning heat at the tip of the toes from this boiling pot of unfamiliar vocabularies, constantly being presented with new concepts, techniques, and frameworks. but this feels exciting. exciting because there are so many things I don’t yet know, that i can keep learning. i recently heard that happiness is not the achieving of a goal; it is the pursuing of it. and im constantly reminded to take each day in this summer as is — to enjoy my process of pursuing. thank you for reading thus far, and hopefully will be back with more thorough reflection and takeaways. #LinkedInLife #LinkedInterns #LinkedIn #AIInfra #GPU
